Curious
KYOOR-ee-us
adjective
From Latin curiosus, “careful, diligent, made with care,” from cura, “care.” The English word first meant made with care — wrought with pains and art; the sense of prying inquisitiveness is a later branch of the same root of care.

Biblical Definition

In the KJV curious means skilfully and carefully wrought — elaborate, made with pains and art. The modern reader hears the word and thinks of a prying mind: the curious child, the curious onlooker, the itch to know. But in the Authorized Version curious is almost never about the mind that inquires; it is about the work that is finely made. The “curious girdle of the ephod” (Exo 29:5) is the intricately woven band that bound the high priest’s vestment — a masterpiece of the loom, not a strange or nosy object. When Bezaleel is gifted “to devise curious works, to work in gold, and in silver, and in brass” (Exo 35:32), the word stands beside cunning as a companion in skill. And the Psalmist adores the God who formed him: he was “made in secret, and curiously wrought in the lowest parts of the earth” (Psa 139:15) — the body is God’s embroidery, needled together in the dark with unspeakable care. There is one place where the word turns dark: the “curious arts” of Ephesus (Act 19:19) — that is, magic, the meddling craft of sorcery, whose books the converts burned. There the curiosity is the forbidden prying into hidden powers that God has fenced off. So the word holds both a holy craft and an unholy one, and the reader must let the context, not his modern instinct, tell him which he is looking at.

Webster 1828 Definition

Made with care and skill; elaborate, finely wrought — not inquisitive.

CURIOUS, wrought with care and art; elaborate; finished with nicety; skilfully made.

From Latin curiosus, from cura, “care.”

The primary sense is made with care; the sense of inquisitive prying is a later branch.

The curious girdle of the ephod was an intricately woven band (Exo 29:5).

The Psalmist was curiously wrought — finely fashioned — in secret (Psa 139:15).

Key Scripture

Psa 139:15 — "My substance was not hid from thee, when I was made in secret, and curiously wrought in the lowest parts of the earth."

Exo 35:32 — "And to devise curious works, to work in gold, and in silver, and in brass,"

Exo 29:5 — "And thou shalt take the garments, and put upon Aaron the coat, and the robe of the ephod, and the ephod, and the breastplate, and gird him with the curious girdle of the ephod:"

Act 19:19 — "Many of them also which used curious arts brought their books together, and burned them before all men: and they counted the price of them, and found it fifty thousand pieces of silver."

Modern Corruption

A word for careful workmanship read as idle nosiness — and, in one place, the honest AV name for forbidden magic.

expand to see more

The honest drift is easy to name: curious once meant made with care and now means eager to know. The modern reader who meets the “curious girdle” pictures a strange or peculiar object, when the text means an exquisitely wrought one. Read it as fine craftsmanship and the tabernacle glows with it — every curious work a labour of skilled and holy hands. The same slide explains Psa 139:15: to be “curiously wrought” is to be embroidered with care in the womb, the most intimate proof of God’s workmanship, not a comment on our inquisitiveness.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. But one biblical use of the word does touch a live and growing evil. The “curious arts” of Act 19:19 are magic: charms, incantations, the meddling craft of sorcery. Ephesus was a capital of it, and the converts proved their repentance by burning fifty thousand pieces of silver’s worth of spell-books in the open street. Our own age has revived exactly this — astrology columns, tarot, crystals, the packaged spirituality that sells the forbidden as harmless self-discovery. Scripture’s word for it all is plain: curious arts, and the fire. The believer is not to dabble at the fence God has set around the hidden things, but to burn the books and cleave to the Word, which tells him all that his Maker means for him to know.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means carefully and skilfully wrought, from the Latin for care.

expand to see more

Curious — from Latin curiosus, from cura, “care.”

In the KJV it means elaborate, finely wrought, made with skill.

The “curious girdle” and “curious works” are craftsmen’s masterpieces.

“Curiously wrought” (Psa 139:15) describes the body embroidered in the womb.

“Curious arts” (Act 19:19) is the one dark sense: forbidden magic.

Usage

"The curious girdle of the ephod was fine weaving, not a peculiar object."

"To be curiously wrought is to be skilfully embroidered — God’s handiwork in the womb."

"The curious arts of Ephesus were magic; the converts burned every book."
